claim: Visual projection neurons (VPNs) provide an anatomical connection between early visual processing and higher brain regions.
source: Visual projection neurons (VPNs) provide an anatomical connection between early visual processing and higher brain regions.
evidence: This is a statement of established anatomical organization in the visual system, drawing from general knowledge of neural architecture.

claim: 22 different LC types were anatomically described in this study.
source: Here we characterize lobula columnar (LC) cells, a class of Drosophila VPNs that project to distinct central brain structures called optic glomeruli. We anatomically describe 22 different LC types
evidence: The manuscript explicitly states the number of LC types characterized, which is supported by the anatomical data presented in the figures.

claim: Optogenetic activation of several LC types evokes specific behaviors in freely moving flies.
source: show that, for several types, optogenetic activation in freely moving flies evokes specific behaviors.
evidence: This claim is supported by the behavioral experiments described in the manuscript and shown in Figure 8.

claim: The activation phenotypes of two LC types closely resemble natural avoidance behaviors triggered by a visual loom.
source: The activation phenotypes of two LC types closely resemble natural avoidance behaviors triggered by a visual loom.
evidence: This is supported by the behavioral comparisons shown in Figure 11.

claim: LC6 and LC16 respond to looming stimuli as revealed by two-photon calcium imaging.
source: In vivo two-photon calcium imaging reveals that these LC types respond to looming stimuli
evidence: This is directly supported by the calcium imaging data presented in Figure 12.

claim: LC11 responds to the motion of a small object but not to looming stimuli.
source: while another type does not, but instead responds to the motion of a small object.
evidence: This is supported by the calcium imaging data in Figure 12E showing LC11's selective response to small moving objects.

claim: Activation of LC neurons on only one side of the brain can result in attractive or aversive turning behaviors depending on the cell type.
source: Activation of LC neurons on only one side of the brain can result in attractive or aversive turning behaviors depending on the cell type.
evidence: This is supported by the stochastic labeling and activation experiments shown in Figure 13.

claim: LC neurons convey information on the presence and location of visual features relevant for specific behaviors.
source: Our results indicate that LC neurons convey information on the presence and location of visual features relevant for specific behaviors.
evidence: This is an interpretation based on the combined anatomical, behavioral, and physiological data presented throughout the manuscript.

claim: The optic lobe in flies is comprised of four neuropils: lamina, medulla, lobula and lobula plate.
source: In flies, visual information is first processed in the optic lobes, which are comprised of four neuropils called the lamina, medulla, lobula and lobula plate (Fischbach and Dittrich, 1989; Meinertzhagen and Hanson, 1993).
evidence: This is established anatomical knowledge supported by the cited references.

claim: Each neuropil in the optic lobe has a repetitive structure of several hundred retinotopically-arranged columns.
source: Each neuropil has a repetitive structure of several hundred retinotopically-arranged columns that support the parallel processing of visual signals from different points in space.
evidence: This is established anatomical knowledge about the organization of the fly visual system.

claim: Neurons projecting out of the optic lobes originate in the medulla, lobula and lobula plate with the majority from the latter two.
source: Neurons projecting out of the optic lobes originate in the medulla, lobula and lobula plate with the majority from the latter two, deeper neuropil layers.
evidence: This is a statement about the anatomical organization of visual projection neurons.

claim: Lobula plate tangential cells (LPTCs) show strongly directionally selective responses to a variety of motion stimuli.
source: These lobula plate tangential cells (LPTCs) show strongly directionally selective responses to a variety of motion stimuli and some LPTCs have been proposed to function as matched filters for the complex optic flow patterns associated with a fly's movements (Krapp et al., 1998).
evidence: This is supported by the cited reference and represents established knowledge about LPTCs.

claim: The vast majority of medulla outputs project to the lobula.
source: A major role of the lobula in visual processing is also indicated by anatomy, since the vast majority of medulla outputs project to the lobula (Fischbach and Dittrich, 1989).
evidence: This is supported by the cited anatomical study.

claim: LC neurons can be divided into over twenty distinct types.
source: The LC neurons are the most numerous VPNs of the lobula and, as we show here, can be divided into over twenty distinct types.
evidence: This is supported by the anatomical characterization presented in the manuscript.

claim: Individual LC neuron dendritic arbors spread across only part of the array of lobula columns.
source: Each LC type comprises multiple neurons of similar morphology whose individual dendritic arbors spread across only part of the array of lobula columns
evidence: This is demonstrated by the anatomical data shown in Figures 1, 6, and related figures.

claim: LC neurons as populations cover the entire visual field with a few exceptions.
source: but which, with a few exceptions, cover the entire visual field as a population (Fischbach and Dittrich, 1989; Otsuna and Ito, 2006; Strausfeld and Okamura, 2007) (Figure 1C,F,K).
evidence: This is supported by both cited references and the anatomical data presented in the manuscript.

claim: The axons of LC neurons converge onto cell-type specific target regions in the central brain.
source: In addition to their dendritic arrangements, the second anatomical hallmark of most LC neurons is the convergence of their axons onto cell-type specific target regions in the central brain (Otsuna and Ito, 2006; Strausfeld and Okamura, 2007).
evidence: This is supported by the cited references and the anatomical data in Figure 3.

claim: Optic glomeruli are enriched for synaptic sites and can be directly visualized with general neuropil markers.
source: Similar to olfactory glomeruli, the optic glomeruli are enriched for synaptic sites and can be directly visualized with general neuropil markers (Figure 1D,E) (Ito et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by the cited reference and demonstrated in Figure 1D,E.

claim: The most prominent optic glomeruli are found in the ventrolateral central brain, specifically the PVLP and PLP.
source: The most prominent of these optic glomeruli are found in the ventrolateral central brain, specifically the posterior ventrolateral protocerebrum (PVLP) and the posterior lateral protocerebrum (PLP) (Figure 1B).
evidence: This is demonstrated by the anatomical data shown in Figure 1B and Figure 3.

claim: The AOTu is considered a specialized optic glomerulus and receives LC cell inputs.
source: In addition, a small dorsal brain region with a glomerular structure, the anterior optic tubercle (AOTu) (Figure 1B), is considered a specialized optic glomerulus and also receives LC cell inputs (Otsuna and Ito, 2006; Strausfeld and Okamura, 2007).
evidence: This is supported by the cited references and the anatomical data presented in the manuscript.

claim: Seven of the LC types characterized in this study (LC4, LC6, LC9-LC13) have been previously described.
source: Seven of these LC types (LC4, LC6, LC9-LC13) have been previously described (Fischbach and Dittrich, 1989; Otsuna and Ito, 2006).
evidence: This is supported by the cited references.

claim: Each of the 22 LC types has morphologically distinct dendritic arbors in the lobula with stereotyped arbor stratification, size and shape.
source: We found that each of the 22 LC types described here has morphologically distinct dendritic arbors in the lobula with stereotyped arbor stratification, size and shape.
evidence: This is supported by the anatomical data presented in Figures 5, 6, and 7.

claim: Arbors of LC neurons are found in all lobula strata, though with large differences between layers.
source: Arbors of LC neurons are found in all lobula strata, though with large differences between layers.
evidence: This is demonstrated by the layer pattern analysis shown in Figure 5.

claim: Only LC4 (and perhaps LPLC1 and LPLC2) cells are potentially postsynaptic to neurons in the most distal lobula layer, Lo1.
source: Only LC4 (and perhaps LPLC1 and LPLC2) cells are potentially postsynaptic to neurons in the most distal lobula layer, Lo1
evidence: This is based on the layer pattern analysis shown in Figure 5.

claim: LC6 and LC16 showed stronger responses to a dark expanding disc than to related stimuli such as an expanding bright disk or a darkening stimulus that lacks the expanding motion.
source: LC6 and LC16 showed stronger responses to a dark expanding disc than to related stimuli such as an expanding bright disk or a darkening stimulus that lacks the expanding motion.
evidence: This is supported by the calcium imaging data in Figure 12D.

claim: LC6 and LC16 have very similar lobula layer patterns while LC11 has a different arbor stratification.
source: Consistent with their similar responses in the imaging experiments, LC6 and LC16 have very similar lobula layer patterns while LC11 has a different arbor stratification
evidence: This is demonstrated by the anatomical data in Figure 5 and Figure 11B.

claim: Most LC neurons largely discard retinotopic information at the glomerulus level.
source: These experiments revealed no detectable retinotopy of LC cell processes in most glomeruli even at this cellular level of resolution.
evidence: This is supported by the MCFO labeling experiments shown in Figure 4.

claim: LC10 cells retain some retinotopic information in the arrangement of their axon terminals.
source: Unlike the other LC neurons, we found that LC10, and to a lesser extent LC9, cells retain some retinotopic information in the arrangement of their axon terminals
evidence: This is demonstrated by the MCFO labeling data in Figure 4H-M.

claim: The order of LC10 axonal terminals in the AOTu along the DV axis matches the sequence of AP positions of the corresponding dendrites in the lobula.
source: we observed that the order of LC10 axonal terminals in the AOTu along the DV axis matches the sequence of AP positions of the corresponding dendrites in the lobula.
evidence: This is demonstrated by the anatomical data in Figure 4H-M.

claim: Activation of different types of LC neurons can induce distinct behaviors including jumping, reaching, wing extension, forward walking, backward walking and turning.
source: We found that activation of different types of LC neurons can induce distinct behaviors including jumping, reaching, wing extension, forward walking, backward walking and turning.
evidence: This is supported by the behavioral data presented in Figure 8.

claim: Five different cell types (LC4, LC6, LC15, LPLC1 and LPLC2) drove highly penetrant jumping in at least one of the two behavioral assays.
source: For example, five different cell types (LC4, LC6, LC15, LPLC1 and LPLC2) drove highly penetrant jumping in at least one of the two assays.
evidence: This is supported by the behavioral data in Figure 8.

claim: LPLC2 activation elicited both jumping and backward walking behaviors with about equal penetrance in the arena assay.
source: For example, LPLC2 activation elicited both jumping and backward walking behaviors with about equal penetrance in the arena assay.
evidence: This is supported by the behavioral data in Figure 8C.

claim: Nearly half of LC neuron types (10/22) drove one of the five assessed behaviors in a majority of flies tested when activated.
source: Overall, when activated, nearly half of LC neuron types (10/22) drove one of the five behaviors we assessed in a majority of flies tested.
evidence: This is based on the behavioral screen results summarized in Figure 8.

claim: CsChrimson activation of LC6 and LC16 lines in norpA mutant flies produced the same behaviors as seen in non-norpA flies.
source: We combined our split-GAL4 driver lines with a norpA mutation that renders the fly blind. CsChrimson activation of these lines produced the same behaviors as seen in non-norpA flies (Figure 9 and Supplementary file 1B)
evidence: This is supported by the control experiments shown in Figure 9.

claim: Parental lines that do not express CsChrimson as well as flies reared on food without supplemental retinal show little or no jumping, backward walking or turning in response to red light.
source: Additionally, parental lines that do not express CsChrimson as well as flies reared on food without supplemental retinal show little or no jumping, backward walking or turning in response to red light (mean penetrance of 0% for jumping, 7% for backward walking and 3% for turning) (Figure 9, Figure 9—figure supplement 2 and Supplementary file 1B).
evidence: This is supported by the control experiments shown in Figure 9.

claim: Several additional, genetically different, split-GAL4 driver lines with targeted LC6 or LC16 expression produced the same, highly penetrant jumping or backward walking and turning behaviors.
source: We also tested several additional, genetically different, split-GAL4 driver lines with targeted LC6 or LC16 expression (Figure 9—figure supplement 1) and found that these lines produced the same, highly penetrant jumping or backward walking and turning behaviors (Figure 9, Figure 9—figure supplement 2 and Supplementary file 1B; 80–100% penetrance for jumping, 89–95% for backward walking and 29–36% for turning).
evidence: This is supported by the data in Figure 9 and related supplements.

claim: LC10 can be divided into four subtypes that each has a distinct layer pattern in the lobula.
source: Unlike other LC cell types, LC10 can be divided into four subtypes that each has a distinct layer pattern in the lobula (Figure 5F)
evidence: This is supported by the anatomical data in Figure 5F and Figure 10.

claim: Activation of LC10a or LC10d neurons alone is sufficient to drive highly penetrant reaching behavior.
source: Thus, activation of LC10a or LC10d neurons alone is sufficient to drive highly penetrant reaching behavior.
evidence: This is supported by the behavioral data in Figure 10D showing specific driver lines for LC10a and LC10d.

claim: LC6 and LC16 are examples of LC cell types that have very similar arbor stratification in the lobula, but project to distinct optic glomeruli.
source: By contrast, LC6 and LC16 are examples of LC cell types that have very similar arbor stratification in the lobula, but project to distinct optic glomeruli (Figure 11A,B, also see Figures 3, 5 and Video 1 and 2).
evidence: This is demonstrated by the anatomical data in Figures 3, 5, and 11.

claim: LC6 depolarization results in a behavior very closely resembling a looming-evoked escape response.
source: Strikingly, the CsChrimson-mediated LC6 depolarization not only produced a takeoff with this same sequence of events (Figure 11C), but the duration of the takeoff sequence was more similar to that of a looming-evoked takeoff than a voluntary one performed when no stimulus was present (Figure 11D). Thus, LC6 depolarization results in a behavior very closely resembling a looming-evoked escape response.
evidence: This is supported by the behavioral comparison data in Figure 11C-D.

claim: Backward walking is a possible response to a specific type of looming stimulus presented in front of the fly at 0° azimuth.
source: In another set of experiments, we found that backward walking is also a possible response to a specific type of looming stimulus. When a fast-approaching looming stimulus was presented in front of the fly at 0° azimuth, many of the flies that did not take off during the observation period instead responded with a backward walking behavior (174/200 flies) similar to that induced by optogenetic depolarization of LC16 (Figure 11E).
evidence: This is supported by the behavioral data in Figure 11E-F.

claim: Looming and LC16 depolarization both caused flies to move backward with similar speeds.
source: We found that looming and LC16 depolarization both caused flies to move backward, and they do so with similar speeds.
evidence: This is supported by the behavioral comparison data in Figure 11F.

claim: Calcium signals integrated over each of the LC6 and LC16 glomeruli both show similar increases in response to dark looming disks.
source: Calcium signals integrated over each of the LC6 and LC16 glomeruli both show similar increases in response to dark looming disks (Figure 12D, top row).
evidence: This is supported by the calcium imaging data in Figure 12D.

claim: Both LC6 and LC16 appear similarly tuned, responding with larger calcium increments to the slower looming speeds presented.
source: Both cell types appear similarly tuned, responding with larger calcium increments to the slower looming speeds presented (Figure 12—figure supplement 1, top row).
evidence: This is supported by the calcium imaging data in Figure 12—figure supplement 1.

claim: Both LC6 and LC16 are selective to dark looming stimuli as a looming disk that was brighter than the background did not elicit large responses.
source: Both cell types are selective to dark looming stimuli as a looming disk that was brighter than the background did not elicit large responses (Figure 12D and Figure 12—figure supplement 1, middle row).
evidence: This is supported by the calcium imaging data in Figure 12D.

claim: A luminance-matched stimulus that darkened over time with the same temporal profile as the dark looming disk, but lacked any coherent edge motion, elicited moderate responses in both LC6 and LC16 that were significantly smaller than the dark looming disk.
source: This stimulus elicited moderate responses in both cell types that were significantly smaller than the dark looming disk (Figure 12D and Figure 12—figure supplement 1, bottom row; Mann-Whitney test, p<0.01 for both LC6 and LC16), indicating their selectivity for stimuli with looming motion.
evidence: This is supported by the calcium imaging data and statistical analysis in Figure 12D.

claim: LC11 did not show calcium response changes to any of the looming-related stimuli.
source: LC11 did not show calcium response changes to any of the looming-related stimuli (Figure 12D and Figure 12—figure supplement 1, black trace).
evidence: This is supported by the calcium imaging data in Figure 12D.

claim: LC11 showed large responses to a small moving object, and more moderate responses to a moving bar spanning the visual display.
source: However, we observed large responses from LC11, when we presented simpler moving stimuli that did not contain looming motion. LC11 showed large responses to a small moving object, and more moderate responses to a moving bar spanning our visual display (Figure 12E).
evidence: This is supported by the calcium imaging data in Figure 12E.

claim: LC6 and LC16 showed calcium responses to the small object, but these responses were smaller than those to the loom stimuli, and much smaller than those of LC11.
source: In contrast, LC6 and LC16 also showed calcium responses to the small object, but these responses were smaller than those to the loom stimuli, and much smaller than those of LC11 (Figure 12E, Mann-Whitney test, p<0.01 for both LC6 and LC16).
evidence: This is supported by the calcium imaging data and statistical analysis in Figure 12E.

claim: Unilateral LC16 optogenetic depolarization only rarely resulted in backward walking, but instead generated strong turning responses.
source: Unlike bilateral activation, unilateral LC16 optogenetic depolarization only rarely resulted in backward walking (Figure 13B), but instead generated strong turning responses (Figure 13C and Video 7).
evidence: This is supported by the stochastic activation data in Figure 13B-C.

claim: Unilateral LC16 activation resulted in turning predominantly away from the activated side.
source: This turning behavior had a strong directional bias with turns predominantly away from the activated side (Figure 13C), suggesting a directional avoidance response.
evidence: This is supported by the behavioral data in Figure 13C.

claim: Unilateral activation of LC10 caused a strong turning bias in the opposite direction from LC16, with flies predominantly making turns toward the activated side.
source: Interestingly, unilateral activation of LC10 also caused a strong turning bias, but in the opposite direction; flies predominantly made turns toward the activated side and the most common LC10 activation phenotypes were now turning responses rather than reaching (Figure 13C).
evidence: This is supported by the behavioral data in Figure 13C.

claim: Each of the 12 most prominent glomeruli in the PVLP is the target of one columnar VPN type from the lobula.
source: In particular, our data show that each of the 12 most prominent glomeruli in the PVLP (or, in one case, the boundary region of PVLP and PLP) (Figure 3B,C, Video 1) is the target of one columnar VPN type from the lobula.
evidence: This is supported by the anatomical mapping data in Figure 3.

claim: Ten of the twelve most prominent PVLP glomeruli are the targets of typical LC cell types while two glomeruli receive inputs of neurons with dendrites in both lobula and lobula plate (LPLC1 and LPLC2).
source: Ten of these glomeruli are the targets of typical LC cell types while two glomeruli receive inputs of neurons with dendrites in both lobula and lobula plate; we refer to these LC-like cells as LPLC1 and LPLC2.
evidence: This is supported by the anatomical data in Figure 3 and related figures.

claim: LC neurons are the primary inputs to the most prominent optic glomeruli in the PVLP.
source: Although we visually screened the expression patterns of several thousand GAL4 lines, we did not observe additional cases where the terminal fields of a VPN similarly coincided with one of these glomeruli (as defined by anti-Brp labeling), suggesting that LC neurons are the primary inputs to these structures.
evidence: This is based on the extensive GAL4 line screening and anatomical mapping presented in the manuscript.

claim: Most individual LC neurons have branched terminals that appear to spread throughout their target glomerulus without obvious spatial restriction to subregions.
source: These experiments revealed that most individual LC neurons, with the exceptions discussed below, had branched terminals that appeared to spread throughout their target glomerulus without obvious spatial restriction to subregions or correlation between the distributions of their dendritic arbors in the lobula and their presynaptic arbors in the glomerulus.
evidence: This is supported by the MCFO labeling data in Figure 4.

claim: LC9 is an example of a cell type that appeared to retain some retinotopy, though with very low spatial resolution, at the level of the axonal terminals.
source: LC9 is an example of a cell type that appeared to retain some retinotopy, though with very low spatial resolution, at the level of the axonal terminals: terminals of single LC9 cells expanded through only part of the glomerulus and their position correlated with the approximate position of the corresponding dendrites in the lobula (Figure 4D–G).
evidence: This is supported by the MCFO labeling data in Figure 4D-G.

claim: The AOTu is innervated by multiple LC cell types that preserve some retinotopy.
source: The most striking example of retinotopy within a glomerulus was the arrangement of the terminals of the LC10 neurons that project to the AOTu (Figure 4H–M).
evidence: This is supported by the anatomical data in Figure 4H-M.

claim: LC10 cells have branched terminals similar to other LC neurons but with limited dorso-ventral (DV) spread so that individual cells did not cover the entire AOTu along this axis.
source: LC10 cells have branched terminals similar to other LC neurons but with limited dorso-ventral (DV) spread so that individual cells did not cover the entire AOTu along this axis (Figure 4I,J,L,M).
evidence: This is demonstrated by the anatomical data in Figure 4I,J,L,M.

claim: In the AOTu, the relative positions of presynaptic arborizations of LC10 cells along the DV axis of the AOTu largely matched the order of their dendrites along the anterior-posterior (AP) axis of the lobula.
source: In the AOTu, the relative positions of presynaptic arborizations of LC10 cells along the DV axis of the AOTu largely matched the order of their dendrites along the anterior-posterior (AP) axis of the lobula (Figure 4H,K), though with more overlap between arbors in the AOTu compared to the lobula.
evidence: This is supported by the anatomical data in Figure 4H,K.

claim: The AOTu is the target of axonal projections of several anatomically distinct LC10 subtypes.
source: LC10 cells also differed in a second key respect from LC cell types innervating most other optic glomeruli; consistent with previous reports (Otsuna and Ito, 2006), we found that the AOTu is the target of axonal projections of several anatomically distinct LC10 subtypes.
evidence: This is supported by the anatomical data in Figures 5F, 10, and related figures, as well as the cited reference.

claim: The classification of LC10 cells is mainly based on the size and layer patterns of the lobula arbors of these neurons.
source: Our classification of LC10 cells is mainly based on the size and layer patterns of the lobula arbors of these neurons
evidence: This is described in the methods and results sections and demonstrated in Figure 5F and Figure 10.

claim: All LC10 types labeled by the driver lines projected to the large medial zone of the AOTu.
source: all LC10 types labeled by our driver lines projected to the large medial zone (Ito et al., 2014) of the AOTu (Figure 3G–I)
evidence: This is supported by the anatomical data in Figure 3G-I and the cited reference.

claim: The axonal terminals of both LC10a and LC10d subtypes are retinotopically distributed along the full DV axis of the AOTu.
source: Our analyses of retinotopy of LC10 neurons using subtypes specific split-GAL4 lines showed that the axonal terminals of both LC10a (Figure 4H–J) and LC10d (Figure 4K–M) subtypes are retinotopically distributed along the full DV axis of the AOTu
evidence: This is supported by the anatomical data in Figure 4H-M.

claim: Different LC10 subtypes form independent retinotopic maps that each cover the entire visual field.
source: suggesting that different subtypes form independent retinotopic maps that each cover the entire visual field.
evidence: This is an interpretation based on the retinotopy data for LC10 subtypes.

claim: The lobula has a distinctly stratified structure.
source: Similar to other optic lobe neuropils, the lobula has a distinctly stratified structure (Fischbach and Dittrich, 1989; Strausfeld, 1976).
evidence: This is established anatomical knowledge supported by the cited references.

claim: Anti-Brp staining in the lobula shows seven bands of alternating labeling intensity that largely correspond to the previously described lobula layers Lo1 to Lo6.
source: In the lobula, anti-Brp staining shows seven bands of alternating labeling intensity (Figure 5A); examination of processes of identified neurons with known positions in the lobula indicated that these anti-Brp strata largely correspond to the previously described (Fischbach and Dittrich, 1989) lobula layers Lo1 to Lo6 (Figure 5A and Figure 5—figure supplement 1), with Lo5 represented by two anti-Brp bands of different intensity.
evidence: This is supported by the anatomical data in Figure 5A and Figure 5—figure supplement 1, as well as the cited reference.

claim: For a given LC type, layer patterns were similar throughout the lobula but differed for cells of different types.
source: Comparison of the layer patterns of different LC cell types, each visualized using a specific split-GAL4 driver line, with the anti-Brp label indicated that, for a given type, layer patterns were similar throughout the lobula (Figure 5B,C) but differed for cells of different types (Figure 5B–D).
evidence: This is supported by the anatomical data in Figure 5B-D.

claim: For nearly all LC neuron types, the layer patterns of individual cells that projected to the same target glomerulus were similar to each other and matched the overall layer patterns seen by labeling the entire cell populations.
source: However, for nearly all LC neuron types, we found that the layer patterns of individual cells that projected to the same target glomerulus were similar to each other and matched the overall layer patterns seen by labeling the entire cell populations using the type-specific split-GAL4 driver lines (compare LC4 and LC15 patterns in Figure 5E and D, respectively; also see Figure 7—figure supplement 1 for examples of single cell labeling of lobula dendrites for all LC cell types).
evidence: This is supported by the comparison of population and single-cell labeling data in Figure 5D-E and Figure 7—figure supplement 1.

claim: Nearly all optic glomeruli receive input from a single LC neuron type that can be recognized independently by either the dendritic arbor stratification in the lobula or the axonal projection pattern.
source: These results indicate that nearly all optic glomeruli receive input from a single LC neuron type that can be recognized independently by either the dendritic arbor stratification in the lobula or the axonal projection pattern.
evidence: This is an interpretation based on the combined anatomical data showing correspondence between layer patterns and target glomeruli.

claim: All lobula layers contain processes of at least one LC cell type, although the number of types contributing to each layer varies widely.
source: We found that all lobula layers contain processes of at least one LC cell type, although the number of types contributing to each layer varies widely.
evidence: This is supported by the layer pattern analysis in Figure 5.

claim: Only LC4 cells have processes in layer Lo1.
source: At one extreme, only LC4 cells have processes in layer Lo1
evidence: This is supported by the layer pattern data in Figure 5D.

claim: All but three LC (LC4, LC12 and LC18) cell types have processes in layer Lo5.
source: by contrast, all but three LC (LC4, LC12 and LC18) cell types have processes in layer Lo5.
evidence: This is supported by the layer pattern data in Figure 5D.

claim: For several LC cell types the presynaptic marker (syt-smHA) used to visualize the target regions was also detectable, though much more weakly, in one or more lobula layers.
source: In addition, the lobula arbors of some LC neurons may be not only postsynaptic but also make some presynaptic contacts; we found that for several LC cell types the presynaptic marker (syt-smHA) used to visualize the target regions was also detectable, though much more weakly, in one or more lobula layers (Figure 5—figure supplement 2, Supplementary file 1A)
evidence: This is supported by the anatomical data in Figure 5—figure supplement 2.

claim: The lateral spread of individual LC neuron arbors in the lobula shows considerable cell-type specific variation.
source: Like layer patterns, lateral dendritic spread is also a stereotyped characteristic of LC neurons with functional implications. As populations, the dendrites of each of the LC neuron types form retinotopic arrays that cover the entire lobula (see Figure 1C,F,K). However, the lateral spread of individual LC neuron arbors in the lobula shows considerable cell-type specific variation (Figure 6 and Figure 6—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by the anatomical data in Figure 6 and Figure 6—figure supplement 1.

claim: The lateral spread of the lobula arbors of cells of all LC types covered lobula regions corresponding to several of the ~750 visual columns within each eye.
source: The lateral spread of the lobula arbors of cells of all LC types covered lobula regions corresponding to several of the ~750 visual columns within each eye.
evidence: This is supported by the anatomical measurements and estimates described in the manuscript.

claim: The largest arbor spreads were observed for LC11, estimated to be over 60 columns.
source: The largest arbor spreads were observed for LC11, estimated to be over 60 columns (Figure 6A and Supplementary file 1A)
evidence: This is supported by the anatomical data in Figure 6A and Supplementary file 1A.

claim: The smallest arbors were those of LC10a (~10 columns).
source: The smallest arbors were those of LC10a (~10 columns; Figure 6B and Supplementary file 1A).
evidence: This is supported by the anatomical data in Figure 6B and Supplementary file 1A.

claim: The distinct arbor spreads of different LC cells determine the spatial extent over which their specific response properties are computed.
source: Since most LC cell types did not show obvious retinotopy within their target glomeruli, we propose that the distinct arbor spreads of different LC cells determine the spatial extent over which their specific response properties are computed, rather than provide retinotopic information at different spatial resolutions.
evidence: This is an interpretation based on the anatomical data showing different arbor sizes and lack of retinotopy in most glomeruli.

claim: The dendrites of a given LC type, with the possible exception of the small arbors of LC10a, do not show a strict tiling pattern but rather overlap.
source: Taken together, our estimates of the number of LC cells of each type and their approximate dendritic arbor spread within lobula layers suggest that the dendrites of a given LC type, with the possible exception of the small arbors of LC10a, do not show a strict tiling pattern but rather overlap (Supplementary file 1A).
evidence: This is based on the anatomical measurements and cell counts presented in the manuscript.

claim: Overlap between processes of cells of the same LC type was directly observed in MCFO experiments for nearly all LC cell types.
source: We also directly observed overlap of co-labeled cells in MCFO experiments (some examples can be found in Figure 6—figure supplement 1) for nearly all LC cell types (Supplementary file 1A).
evidence: This is supported by the MCFO labeling data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1.

claim: The multicolumnar arbor span, intricate arbor shapes and diverse and multistratified layer patterns of LC neurons suggest that these neurons spatially integrate inputs from multiple presynaptic cells of several types.
source: In summary, the multicolumnar arbor span (Figure 6 and Figure 6—figure supplement 1), intricate arbor shapes (Figure 7, Figure 7—figure supplements 1 and 2) and diverse and, in most cases, multistratified layer patterns (Figure 5, Figure 7—figure supplements 1 and 2) of LC neurons, suggest that these neurons spatially integrate inputs from multiple presynaptic cells of several types.
evidence: This is an interpretation based on the anatomical features of LC neurons.

claim: The population of LC cell types has the potential to encode a diversity of visual stimuli, with large differences expected between distinct types.
source: These anatomical characteristics suggest that as a whole, the population of LC cell types has the potential to encode a diversity of visual stimuli, with large differences expected between distinct types.
evidence: This is an interpretation based on the diverse anatomical properties of different LC types.

claim: The anatomical reorganization resulting from the convergence of LC axons into largely cell-type specific glomeruli has led to the speculation that the activity of members of a given LC cell type primarily signals the presence of a particular behaviorally relevant visual feature rather than its precise location.
source: As discussed in the Introduction, the anatomical reorganization resulting from the convergence of LC axons into largely cell-type specific glomeruli, has led to the speculation (Mu et al., 2012; Strausfeld and Okamura, 2007) that the activity of members of a given LC cell type primarily signals the presence of a particular behaviorally relevant visual feature rather than its precise location.
evidence: This is a hypothesis from the literature supported by the cited references.

claim: Strong artificial activation of an individual LC cell type might elicit a behavioral response that could provide clues to the function of these neurons.
source: Thus, it is reasonable to expect that strong artificial activation of an individual LC neuronal cell type might elicit a behavioral response that could provide clues to the function of these neurons.
evidence: This is a logical inference that motivated the optogenetic activation experiments.

claim: Red light activation of CsChrimson in LC neurons resulted in several phenotypes that were dramatically different from baseline responses in control flies.
source: However, we found that red light activation of CsChrimson in LC neurons resulted in several phenotypes that were dramatically different from these baseline responses (Videos 3–6).
evidence: This is supported by the behavioral data in Figure 8 and related videos.

claim: The relationship between LC neuron type activated and observed behavior was not one-to-one.
source: We found that the relationship between LC neuron type activated and observed behavior was not one-to-one.
evidence: This is based on the behavioral screen results showing multiple behaviors from single cell types and vice versa.

claim: The jumping phenotype of the LC4 and LPLC1 lines had much higher penetrance in the single-fly assay than in the arena assay.
source: For example, the jumping phenotype of the LC4 and LPLC1 lines had much higher penetrance in the single-fly assay than in the arena assay
evidence: This is supported by the comparison of behavioral data between the two assays in Figure 8C,D.

claim: The forward walking phenotype of the LC24 split-GAL4 driver had higher penetrance in the arena assay than in the single-fly assay.
source: whereas the opposite was the case for the forward walking phenotype of the LC24 split-GAL4 driver (Figure 8C,D).
evidence: This is supported by the comparison of behavioral data between the two assays in Figure 8C,D.

claim: CsChrimson-mediated acute depolarization of individual LC cell types can induce diverse, cell-type specific behavioral responses.
source: The screen results suggest that CsChrimson-mediated acute depolarization of individual LC cell types can induce diverse, cell-type specific behavioral responses.
evidence: This is a summary interpretation of the behavioral screen results.

claim: The distinct LC6 and LC16 phenotypes observed in the screen are due to the experimental activation of these cell types.
source: These results confirm that the distinct LC6 and LC16 phenotypes observed in the screen are due to the experimental activation of these cell types.
evidence: This is supported by the control experiments in Figure 9.

claim: An independent thermogenetic activation screen of more than 2000 lines from the Janelia GAL4 collection also identified the LC6 and LC16 cell types as producing the jumping and backward walking phenotypes.
source: Furthermore, an independent thermogenetic activation screen of more than 2000 lines from the Janelia GAL4 collection also identified the LC6 and LC16 cell types as producing the jumping and backward walking phenotypes through correlation between behavior and anatomy (A A Robie and K Branson, personal communication, September 2016).
evidence: This is supported by independent unpublished data from other researchers.

claim: Activation of specific LC neuron types can result in highly penetrant, cell-type specific behavioral responses.
source: Thus, activation of specific LC neuron types can result in highly penetrant, cell-type specific behavioral responses.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion based on the behavioral data.

claim: The expression patterns of the LC10 lines with the strongest reaching behavior appeared to differ from those of the other lines by having denser processes in more distal lobula layers (mainly ~ Lo3 and Lo4).
source: Consistent with possible functional differences between LC10 subtypes in these experiments, we found that the expression patterns of the lines with the strongest reaching behavior appeared to differ from those of the other lines by having denser processes in more distal lobula layers (mainly ~ Lo3 and Lo4) (Figure 10B).
evidence: This is supported by the anatomical and behavioral correlation data in Figure 10B.

claim: LC10a and/or LC10d cells were found in all lines with strong reaching phenotypes.
source: We found LC10a and/or LC10d cells in all lines with strong reaching phenotypes (Figure 10C,D and Figure 10—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is supported by the MCFO labeling and behavioral data in Figure 10 and Figure 10—figure supplement 2.

claim: The lines with weaker reaching phenotypes showed labeling of LC10b and LC10c cells and little or no expression in the other two LC10 subtypes.
source: The lines with weaker reaching phenotypes showed labeling of LC10b and LC10c cells and little or no expression in the other two LC10 subtypes
evidence: This is supported by the MCFO labeling and behavioral data in Figure 10 and Figure 10—figure supplement 2.

claim: LC10b and LC10c neurons only have a minor, if any, role in generating the reaching behavior.
source: further suggesting that, unlike LC10a or LC10d, LC10b and LC10c neurons only have a minor, if any, role in generating the reaching behavior.
evidence: This is an interpretation based on the correlation between subtype expression and behavioral phenotypes.

claim: LC6 and LC16 show different, highly penetrant, activation-induced behaviors—jumping and backward walking, respectively.
source: Despite the similarity in their lobula arbors, LC6 and LC16 show different, highly penetrant, activation-induced behaviors—jumping and backward walking, respectively (Figure 11B and Videos 4–6).
evidence: This is supported by the behavioral data in Figure 8 and Figure 11.

claim: For the flies that took off in response to the looming stimulus at 90° azimuth (47/174 flies), a consistent, coordinated behavioral sequence was observed that started with the fly beginning to elevate its wings, followed by rapid middle (jumping) leg extension and initiation of flight.
source: For the flies that took off in response to the looming stimulus at 90° azimuth (47/174 flies) we observed a consistent, coordinated behavioral sequence that started with the fly beginning to elevate its wings, followed by rapid middle (jumping) leg extension and initiation of flight as previously described (Figure 11C) (Card and Dickinson, 2008b; von Reyn et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by the behavioral observations and cited references.

claim: Flies perform the same takeoff sequence when taking off voluntarily, however the elevation of their wings is slower, resulting in a significantly longer-duration takeoff sequence than those evoked by looming stimuli.
source: Flies perform the same sequence when taking off voluntarily, however the elevation of their wings is slower (Card and Dickinson, 2008a), resulting in a significantly longer-duration takeoff sequence than those evoked by looming stimuli.
evidence: This is supported by the cited reference and the behavioral comparison data.

claim: Neither LC6 nor LC16 appeared to be essential for the assayed looming-evoked behaviors based on Kir2.1 silencing experiments.
source: Neither cell type appeared to be essential for the assayed behaviors: No reduction of backward walking compared to controls was observed for LC16 (Figure 11—figure supplement 1C) and a reduced jump frequency when blocking LC6 was apparent only for the fast loom (Figure 11—figure supplement 1A). However, no difference in takeoff sequence duration was observed (Figure 11—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is supported by the silencing experiments in Figure 11—figure supplement 1.

claim: Functional redundancy exists at the level of neurons mediating looming-evoked escape.
source: Because multiple LC neuron types show jumping or backward walking responses to optogenetic stimulation (Figure 8) and non-LC cell types have also been reported to contribute to looming-evoked escape (de Vries and Clandinin, 2012), the simplest explanation of these results is that functional redundancy exists at the level of neurons mediating looming-evoked escape.
evidence: This is an interpretation based on the silencing results and knowledge of other neurons involved in escape behaviors.

claim: Looming stimuli evoke responses in several axons that span each LC6 and LC16 glomerulus.
source: In agreement with the anatomical results showing that retinotopy is not simply preserved in the LC6 and LC16 glomeruli (Figure 4A–C, Figure 4—figure supplement 1A–C), we observed that looming stimuli evoke responses in several axons that span each glomerulus (Figure 12C).
evidence: This is supported by the calcium imaging data in Figure 12C.

claim: The reduction in the LC6 and LC16 responses when the edge motion is removed from the stimulus is precisely what is expected of loom-sensitive neurons.
source: The reduction in the LC6 and LC16 responses when the edge motion is removed from the stimulus is precisely what is expected of loom-sensitive neurons and is reminiscent of behavioral studies in houseflies showing that darkening contrast combined with edge motion is the most effective stimulus for triggering takeoffs (Holmqvist and Srinivasan, 1991).
evidence: This is an interpretation based on the calcium imaging data and comparison to behavioral studies in the cited reference.

claim: The selectivity for visual stimuli observed in LC neuron responses is likely both a property of the stimulus selectivity of their inputs and specific computations implemented by individual LC neuron types.
source: It is likely that the selectivity for visual stimuli observed in LC neuron responses is both a property of the stimulus selectivity of their inputs—some selectivity was seen while imaging in the dendrites of a few LC cell types (Aptekar et al., 2015)—and specific computations implemented by individual LC neuron types.
evidence: This is an interpretation based on the imaging data and cited reference.

claim: Cells post-synaptic to the LC cells may integrate the responses of several individual LC neurons of the same type to provide more robust detection of specific visual features.
source: In addition, cells post-synaptic to the LC cells may integrate the responses of several individual LC neurons of the same type to provide more robust detection of specific visual features.
evidence: This is a speculation about downstream processing.

claim: Independent of the presence or absence of retinotopy at the glomerulus level, positional information can be extracted from the differential activity of LC cells between the two optic lobes.
source: We found that, independent of the presence or absence of retinotopy at the glomerulus level, positional information can be extracted from the differential activity of LC cells between the two optic lobes.
evidence: This is supported by the stochastic activation experiments in Figure 13.

claim: LC neuron signaling appears to convey information on both different visual features and their location.
source: Thus, LC neuron signaling appears to convey information on both different visual features and their location.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion based on the combined anatomical, physiological, and behavioral data.

claim: LC neuron signaling may extend the similarities to the antennal lobes where differences in odorant receptor neuron activity between the left and right antennal lobes may contribute to odorant tracking.
source: This may further extend the similarities to the antennal lobes where differences in odorant receptor neuron activity between the left and right antennal lobes may contribute to odorant tracking (Gaudry et al., 2013).
evidence: This is a speculation based on analogy to the olfactory system supported by the cited reference.

claim: A plausible interpretation of the activation results is that activation of LC neurons can mimic the presence of the visual features that these neurons normally respond to and thus elicits behavioral responses associated with these fictive stimuli.
source: A plausible interpretation of these results is that activation of LC neurons can mimic the presence of the visual features that these neurons normally respond to and thus elicits behavioral responses associated with these fictive stimuli.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the combined activation and imaging data.

claim: The encoding of visual information at the level of LC neurons is sufficiently specialized to contribute to distinct behavioral responses in a cell-type dependent fashion.
source: Overall, the LC neuron activation phenotypes we observed suggest that the encoding of visual information at the level of LC neurons is sufficiently specialized to contribute to distinct behavioral responses in a cell-type dependent fashion.
evidence: This is a summary interpretation of the behavioral data.

claim: Patterns of LC neuron activation that produce more refined fictive stimuli than employed in the current work will be required to fully explore the LC neuron behavioral repertoire.
source: However, patterns of LC neuron activation that produce more refined fictive stimuli than we employed in the current work will be required to fully explore the LC neuron behavioral repertoire.
evidence: This is a speculation about future experiments.

claim: In the simplest scenario, LC neuron depolarization could directly activate a single postsynaptic premotor descending interneuron that would then in turn trigger the observed behavior.
source: In the simplest scenario, LC neuron depolarization could directly activate a single postsynaptic premotor descending interneuron that would then in turn trigger the observed behavior.
evidence: This is a speculation about the circuit mechanism.

claim: Activation of LC4 neurons (called ColA cells in larger flies) might evoke a jumping response via activation of the Giant Fiber (GF) cells.
source: This appears plausible in some cases: for example, activation of LC4 neurons (called ColA cells in larger flies) might evoke a jumping response via activation of the Giant Fiber (GF) cells, a pair of large descending neurons known to be postsynaptic to ColA (Strausfeld and Bassemir, 1983) and LC4 (K von Reyn and GM Card, personal communication, September 2016) and which have a known role in escape behavior (von Reyn et al., 2014; Wyman et al., 1984).
evidence: This is a speculation based on anatomical connectivity data from the literature and personal communication.

claim: For other LC cell types, there is currently no evidence suggesting a direct connection to descending neurons.
source: For other LC cell types, there is currently no evidence suggesting a direct connection to descending neurons.
evidence: This is a statement about the current state of knowledge.

claim: Candidate descending neurons for the LC16 backward walking response, the moon-walker descending interneurons, do not have dendrites in or near the LC16 glomerulus.
source: For example, candidate descending neurons for the LC16 backward walking response, the moon-walker descending interneurons (Bidaye et al., 2014), do not have dendrites in or near the LC16 glomerulus.
evidence: This is based on anatomical knowledge from the cited reference.

claim: Responses to diverse visual stimuli, some of which may derive from LC neuron activity, have been observed in higher order brain centers without direct connections to LC neurons such as the central complex.
source: Responses to diverse visual stimuli, some of which may derive from LC neuron activity, have also been observed in higher order brain centers without direct connections to LC neurons such as the central complex (Seelig and Jayaraman, 2013; Weir and Dickinson, 2015).
evidence: This is supported by the cited references.

claim: The signaling downstream of LC neurons is likely to be more complex than a simple direct connection to a single descending neuron.
source: Our activation experiments also provide several indications that the signaling downstream of LC neurons is likely to be more complex
evidence: This is an interpretation based on the complexity of behavioral responses observed.

claim: Activation of a single LC cell type can give rise to multiple behaviors such as reaching, wing extension and turning for LC10, or backward walking and turning for LC16.
source: for example, activation of a single LC cell type can give rise to multiple behaviors such as reaching, wing extension and turning for LC10, or backward walking and turning for LC16.
evidence: This is supported by the behavioral data in Figure 8.

claim: Changes of the spatial pattern of LC neuron activation can modify activation phenotypes.
source: Changes of the spatial pattern of LC neuron activation, as in our stochastic labeling experiments, can further modify activation phenotypes.
evidence: This is supported by the stochastic activation data in Figure 13.

claim: Unilateral LC16 activation primarily evokes turning away from the location of LC16 activation, not backward walking.
source: For example, unilateral LC16 activation primarily evokes turning away from the location of LC16 activation, not backward walking
evidence: This is supported by the stochastic activation data in Figure 13B-C.

claim: The relative differences in LC16 activity between the two eyes can guide the direction of motor output through downstream signaling.
source: suggesting that the relative differences in LC16 activity between the two eyes can guide the direction of motor output through downstream signaling.
evidence: This is an interpretation based on the unilateral activation results.

claim: Several different LC neuron types may contribute to the same or similar behaviors, as suggested by the jumping phenotypes of LC4, LC6, LC15, LPLC1 and LPLC2.
source: Furthermore, several different LC neuron types may contribute to the same or similar behaviors, as suggested by the jumping phenotypes of LC4, LC6, LC15, LPLC1 and LPLC2.
evidence: This is supported by the behavioral data in Figure 8.

claim: Visual signals and other information downstream of LC neurons are presumably integrated to select appropriate behavioral actions.
source: Presumably, visual signals and other information downstream of LC neurons are integrated to select appropriate behavioral actions.
evidence: This is a speculation about downstream processing.

claim: Some responses to LC neuron activation appear to be context dependent.
source: We also note that some responses to LC neuron activation appear to be context dependent; for example, we observed reduced forward walking for several LC cell types on the platform of the single-fly assay that is much smaller than the arena used in the arena assay (Figure 8—figure supplement 1E and F, Supplementary file 1B).
evidence: This is supported by the comparison of behavioral data between the two assays.

claim: LC neuron signaling might have different consequences depending on the behavioral state.
source: In addition, we only examined the behavior of standing or walking flies and LC neuron signaling might have different consequences depending on the behavioral state.
evidence: This is a speculation about context-dependent responses.

claim: Looming stimuli can also elicit avoidance responses in flying flies, but these responses differ from the takeoff or retreat behaviors of walking animals.
source: For example, looming stimuli can also elicit avoidance responses in flying flies (Muijres et al., 2014; Tammero and Dickinson, 2002), but these responses differ from the takeoff or retreat behaviors of walking animals.
evidence: This is supported by the cited references.

claim: While LC cell activity appears to convey visual information that is specialized for sets of related behavioral responses, LC neurons do not appear to instruct a single behavioral output.
source: Therefore, while LC cell activity appears to convey visual information that is specialized for sets of related behavioral responses, LC neurons do not appear to instruct a single behavioral output.
evidence: This is a summary interpretation of the behavioral data.

claim: The most common activation phenotypes observed in the screen were apparent avoidance responses.
source: The most common activation phenotypes observed in our screen were apparent avoidance responses.
evidence: This is based on the behavioral screen results in Figure 8.

claim: In addition to the LC cells studied here, other VPNs may also contribute to avoidance behaviors.
source: Furthermore, in addition to the LC cells studied here, other VPNs may also contribute to avoidance behaviors (de Vries and Clandinin, 2012).
evidence: This is supported by the cited reference.

claim: This predominance of avoidance phenotypes is perhaps not unexpected since escape responses have to be fast and reliably executed under many different conditions.
source: This predominance of avoidance phenotypes is perhaps not unexpected. Since escape responses have to be fast and reliably executed under many different conditions, neurons that signal features that can evoke escape may be particularly likely to show phenotypes in an activation screen.
evidence: This is a speculation about why avoidance phenotypes were common.

claim: It appears plausible that a considerable fraction of visual output neurons might be utilized for the detection of visual threats ranging from looming to small objects.
source: Given the importance of predator avoidance for fly survival, it appears plausible that a considerable fraction of visual output neurons might be utilized for the detection of visual threats ranging from looming to small objects (Card, 2012; Maimon et al., 2008).
evidence: This is a speculation supported by the cited references.

claim: It is likely that CsChrimson-mediated depolarization of an entire population of LC neurons is more similar to the pattern of neuronal activity induced by an imminent collision.
source: Furthermore, it is likely that CsChrimson-mediated depolarization of an entire population of LC neurons is more similar to the pattern of neuronal activity induced by an imminent collision, and thus responses of many individual loom-sensitive neurons, so it is not surprising that our activation screen revealed at least two looming-sensitive neuron types.
evidence: This is a speculation about the nature of the optogenetic stimulus.

claim: The escape-inducing neurons identified could provide inputs to different escape response pathways, such as long- and short-mode escape, or act as multiple inputs to the same downstream circuits.
source: The escape-inducing neurons we identified could provide inputs to different escape response pathways, such as long- and short-mode escape (von Reyn et al., 2014), or act as multiple inputs to the same downstream circuits.
evidence: This is a speculation about the circuit organization supported by the cited reference.

claim: Neurons with avoidance-like activation phenotypes project to two separate groups of adjacent glomeruli, one in the dorsal PVLP (LC6, LC16 and also LC15) and one more ventral and medial (LC4, LPLC1 and LPLC2).
source: Interestingly, neurons with avoidance-like activation phenotypes project to two separate groups of adjacent glomeruli, one in the dorsal PVLP (LC6, LC16 and also LC15) and one more ventral and medial (LC4, LPLC1 and LPLC2).
evidence: This is based on the anatomical data in Figure 3.

claim: This spatial organization may facilitate synaptic interactions of functionally related LC neuron types with common downstream pathways for a specific behavior.
source: This spatial organization may facilitate synaptic interactions of functionally related LC neuron types with common downstream pathways for a specific behavior.
evidence: This is a speculation about the functional significance of the anatomical organization.

claim: The second group of avoidance-related LC neurons is close to dendritic branches of the GF, large descending neurons required for short-mode responses in Drosophila and a postsynaptic partner of LC4/ColA.
source: The second group is close to dendritic branches of the GF, large descending neurons required for short-mode responses in Drosophila and a postsynaptic partner of LC4/ColA (Strausfeld and Bassemir, 1983) (K von Reyn and GM Card, personal communication, September 2016) and possibly also the two LPLC cell types.
evidence: This is based on anatomical knowledge from the cited reference and personal communication.

claim: LC6 terminals do not overlap with GF dendrites and LC6 cells may play a role in the GF-independent escape pathways.
source: LC6 terminals do not overlap with GF dendrites and LC6 cells may play a role in the GF-independent escape pathways that have been proposed in both Drosophila (Fotowat et al., 2009; von Reyn et al., 2014) and housefly (Holmqvist, 1994).
evidence: This is a speculation based on anatomical observations and cited references.

claim: Parallel neuronal pathways involved in escape behaviors have been identified or postulated in both vertebrates and invertebrates.
source: Parallel neuronal pathways involved in escape behaviors have been identified or postulated in both vertebrates and invertebrates (Burrows and Rowell, 1973; Fotowat and Gabbiani, 2011; Fotowat et al., 2011; Münch et al., 2009; Yilmaz and Meister, 2013)
evidence: This is supported by the cited references.

claim: A contribution of several identified visual projection neurons to escape pathways, as suggested by the activation screen, has not been previously reported.
source: but a contribution of several identified visual projection neurons to such pathways, as suggested by our activation screen, has not been previously reported.
evidence: This is a statement about the novelty of the findings.

claim: Different visual output neurons with distinct tuning of their response properties to looming parameters such as speed, size, luminance change or edge detection might have evolved to ensure robust responses to avoid predators or collisions.
source: Different visual output neurons with distinct tuning of their response properties to looming parameters such as speed, size, luminance change or edge detection might have evolved to ensure robust responses to avoid predators or collisions.
evidence: This is a speculation about the evolutionary significance of multiple looming-sensitive neurons.

claim: It is currently not known whether LPLC1, LPLC2, LC4 and LC15 are indeed sensitive to looming stimuli and if so, whether their response details differ from LC16, LC6 and each other.
source: It is, however, currently not known whether LPLC1, LPLC2, LC4 and LC15 are indeed sensitive to looming stimuli and if so, whether their response details differ from LC16, LC6 and each other.
evidence: This is a statement about the current state of knowledge.

claim: The identification of these neurons opens the possibility to examine the potential contribution of several visual pathways to avoidance behaviors.
source: Nevertheless, the identification of these neurons opens the possibility to examine the potential contribution of several visual pathways to avoidance behaviors.
evidence: This is a statement about the implications of the findings for future research.

claim: LC neurons are a subset of the about a hundred VPN cell types that relay the output of optic lobe circuits to targets in the central brain.
source: LC neurons are a subset of the about a hundred VPN cell types that relay the output of optic lobe circuits to targets in the central brain.
evidence: This is a statement about the broader context of LC neurons within the visual system.

claim: The data strongly support existing proposals for LC cell types as feature-detecting neurons, which have been mainly based on the distinct anatomical properties of LC cells.
source: Our data strongly support existing proposals for LC cell types as feature-detecting neurons, which have been mainly based on the distinct anatomical properties of LC cells (Strausfeld and Okamura, 2007).
evidence: This is a summary statement supported by the combined data and the cited reference.

claim: An association of VPN pathways with specific behaviors is not unique to LC cell types.
source: While these anatomical features distinguish LC neurons from many other VPNs, an association of VPN pathways with specific behaviors is not unique to LC cell types.
evidence: This is a statement about the broader context of VPN function.

claim: The notion that individual neuronal pathways are tuned for specific behavioral requirements is a prominent theme in invertebrate neuroethology.
source: The notion that individual neuronal pathways are tuned for specific behavioral requirements is a prominent theme in invertebrate neuroethology, with these neurons described as 'matched filters' for behaviorally relevant features of the external world (Warrant, 2016; Wehner, 1987).
evidence: This is supported by the cited references.

claim: A number of previously studied VPN pathways, outside of the LC subgroup, have been described as encoding specific behaviorally related visual stimuli.
source: A number of previously studied VPN pathways, outside of the LC subgroup, have been described as encoding specific behaviorally related visual stimuli.
evidence: This is a statement about the broader literature on VPNs.

claim: A group of tangential cells of the lobula and lobula plate (Foma-1 neurons) were found to respond to looming visual stimuli and, upon optogenetic activation, trigger escape responses.
source: In particular, very similar to our results for LC6 and LC16, a group of tangential cells of the lobula and lobula plate (Foma-1 neurons) were found to respond to looming visual stimuli and, upon optogenetic activation, trigger escape responses (de Vries and Clandinin, 2012).
evidence: This is supported by the cited reference.

claim: The long-studied LPTCs, such as the HS and VS cells, integrate local motion signals so as to preferentially respond to global optic flow patterns that are remarkably similar to visual motion encountered during specific behavioral movements.
source: And perhaps most famously, the long-studied LPTCs, such as the HS and VS cells, integrate local motion signals so as to preferentially respond to global optic flow patterns that are remarkably similar to visual motion encountered during specific behavioral movements (Hausen, 1976, 1982a; Krapp et al., 1998).
evidence: This is supported by the cited references.

claim: Both the results of this study and previous findings are consistent with the idea that, at the outputs of the fly visual system, we find VPN pathways whose encoding properties are already well matched to particular fly behaviors or groups of behaviors.
source: Both our results and these findings are consistent with the idea that, at the outputs of the fly visual system, we find VPN pathways whose encoding properties are already well matched to particular fly behaviors or groups of behaviors.
evidence: This is a summary interpretation of the findings in the context of the broader literature.

claim: Matching the response properties of these deep sensory circuits to behavioral needs may be a general evolutionary solution to the challenge of dealing with the complexity of the visual world with limited resources.
source: Matching the response properties of these deep sensory circuits to behavioral needs may be a general evolutionary solution to the challenge of dealing with the complexity of the visual world with limited resources.
evidence: This is a speculation about the evolutionary significance of the findings.

claim: LC neurons have long been recognized as a potential entry point for the circuit-level study of visual responses outside of the canonical motion detection pathways.
source: LC neurons have long been recognized as a potential entry point for the circuit-level study of visual responses outside of the canonical motion detection pathways.
evidence: This is a statement about the historical context of LC neuron research.

claim: This study provides a comprehensive anatomical description of LC cell types and genetic reagents to facilitate further investigations.
source: We provide a comprehensive anatomical description of LC cell types and genetic reagents to facilitate such further investigations.
evidence: This is a summary of the contributions of the study.

claim: This work provides a starting point for exploring the circuit mechanisms both upstream and downstream of LC neurons.
source: Our work provides a starting point for exploring the circuit mechanisms both upstream and downstream of LC neurons.
evidence: This is a statement about the implications of the work for future research.
